extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in historical/fictional divination practices and dream interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and prescriptive practices (as given in the narrative) for performing and interpreting divination by Virgilian lots, dice, and dreams — including procedures, dietary and behavioral preparations, interpretive rules, and cautions. Framed in an early-modern/fictional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virgilian-lottery method (selecting a verse by lot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open Virgil at random (the page 'which in the setting open of the book you shall have pitched upon'), then pick a specific line by chance (e.g., by counting to the line number determined by dice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure exemplified: throw three dice, sum the pips (e.g., 5+6+5 = 16) and take that numbered line on the opened page. The text gives many historical examples (emperors finding prophetic lines in Virgil) but cautions against inferring infallibility from such results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-dice line-selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use three fair dice to produce a number which designates the line to be read from the opened page of Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in narrative: three dice cast to 5, 6, and 5 gives 16; take the sixteenth line. Practical notes in dialogue include informal allowances for correcting a first bad throw (tennis 'fifteen' analogy) and that players may adjust their counting if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/legal prohibition of dice and similar lotteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Dice-playing and the play at 'cockall' are characterised as deceitful, abusive, illicitous, and scandalous — to be distrusted and forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel asserts dice are an 'accursed' device (Recreation of Dice) and says his father Gargantua forbade dice, burned moulds, and suppressed such play as a dangerous plague to the commonwealth. The text treats such devices as devilish snares that lead simple souls astray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking gods or ritual paraphernalia for the Virgilian lot
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not perform elaborate invocations of Hercules or the Tenetian goddesses when opening the book; simply open the leaves and use your fingers/nails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel recommends against invoking deities and advises merely to 'open up the leaves of the book with your fingers, and set your nails awork.' The passage also dismisses other superstitious attachments (see amulets below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration across divinatory methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare results from different divinatory practices (e.g., Virgilian lots and dreams) — agreement between methods strengthens the interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative shows Panurge's Virgilian lots and his dream giving corresponding portents (cuckoldry, beating, robbery). The text presents this cross-agreement as a sign of conformity, though also warns against assuming absolute certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a skilled dream-interpreter (oniropolist)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reliable reading of dreams, employ a dexterous, learned, skilful, wise, and expert interpreter (Greek: onirocrit or oniropolist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel emphasises that the soul rarely reports dreams perfectly and so requires an adept interpreter; the passage lists classical authorities to justify the need for expertise in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state required for prophetic dreaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to sleeping for divinatory dreams, the dreamer must denude the mind of passions (love, hatred, fear, hope) so the 'Nous' (mind) is calm, peaceable, and undistracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Proteus: the divine part must be restored to its natural calm for true presaging. Emotional agitation or distracting passions are said to obstruct prophetic reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary and fasting rules for somniatory divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a moderate preparatory diet before attempting prophetic dreams: avoid overeating, extreme fasting, and certain foods; some authorities recommend 24 hours without victuals and three days abstaining from wine, but mediocrity is commended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendations: do not sup heavily; a little supper is allowed but avoid hare, beans, 'preak' (polyp), coleworts, cabbage and other windy foods. Eat pears, a pippin apple, some small plums and cherries; drink pure water. The text warns against both excess and long fasting (long fasting makes spirits 'insipid').

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/environmental conditions for reliable dreaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure bodily comfort (not too hungry nor overfull) and minimize external noise and disturbances to allow the spirit to receive and convey clear visions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel gives a catalogue of noises (dogs, birds, farm animals, etc.) that prevent contemplative work and compares a distracted body to a smudged looking-glass that cannot show a clear image. The sleeping place should be quiet and the dreamer attentive to sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic interpretive rules (examples: horns, metamorphoses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols must be judged by their mythological and cultural associations; the same symbol (e.g., horns) can have multiple meanings (cuckoldry, abundance) and must be interpreted in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The debate over Panurge's horns: Pantagruel reads them as cuckoldry (following Artemidorus); Panurge insists they signify abundance (cornucopia). The passage stresses that interpreters must weigh traditions, myths (Jupiter, Minerva, Amalthaean horn), and alternative senses rather than take images literally (no literal metamorphosis into drum or chough).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ivory vs. horn gates metaphor for dream veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the classical distinction: dreams that come through the gate of horn are true and certain; those through the gate of ivory are confused, doubtful, and false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel mentions Homeric doctrine of two gates: ivory admits doubtful dreams (opacity, confusion), horn admits sure and distinct dreams (diaphanous, transparent). Friar John parodies the notion but the guideline is presented as a traditional rubric for judging dream reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject charms and amulets as unnecessary superstitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on talismans (laurel under pillow, ammonian horn, crocodile shoulder, chameleon, precious stones) to guarantee truthful dreams; these practices are superstitious and their efficacy is disputed by authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel dismisses various folk remedies and amulets, citing writers (Serapion, Antiphon, Fulgentius) who have exposed such cheats; the narrator treats these as unnecessary and suspect.
